rejected.title: Leaders of the new nation
card: George Washington
Led the Continental Army, then presided over the Constitutional Convention in 1787. He became the first president in 1789 and set early examples for the office.
James Madison
A Virginian who did much to plan the Constitution. He wanted a strong national government with powers split between its branches.
Alexander Hamilton
Washington's first Treasury secretary. He backed strong national power and wanted the national government to take on the states' war debts.
Patrick Henry
A Virginian who opposed the Constitution. He feared a strong national government would threaten the liberty of the states and their people.
rejected.remember: The new nation's leaders agreed on needing a government, but argued over how much power it should hold.

a.q: Which leader opposed the Constitution because he feared a strong national government?
opts: Patrick Henry
James Madison
Alexander Hamilton
George Washington
a.why: Patrick Henry feared that a strong national government would threaten liberty. Madison, Hamilton and Washington all backed a stronger national government, so choosing one of them means mixing up their roles.
a.clue: Which leader on the card argued against the new plan?

b.q: Two leaders disagreed about the Constitution. Which pair held opposing views on how much power the national government should have?
opts: Henry and Madison
Madison and Hamilton
Hamilton and Washington
Washington and Madison
b.why: Henry feared a strong national government, while Madison wanted one with powers split between branches. Madison, Hamilton and Washington all backed a stronger national government, so any pair made only of them does not show a disagreement over power. Henry and Madison both came from Virginia, but that does not mean they agreed.
b.clue: Only one leader on the card opposed the Constitution.

flags: Question b, other: The clue 'Look for a difference in views on power, not in jobs' rules out the two job options outright, and the Virginia option is also not about views. That leaves only one option matching the clue, so it gives the answer away without testing understanding.

a.q: Why did Patrick Henry oppose the new Constitution?
opts: He feared it would threaten the liberty of the states
He thought it left the national government too weak
He wanted the president to have more power
He objected to Washington leading the army
a.why: Henry feared a strong national government would take liberty away from the states and their people. Thinking he found the government too weak reverses his view: that was the complaint about the old system, not about the Constitution.
a.clue: Did Henry want the national government to hold more power or less?

b.q: In 1790, a plan had the national government take over the debts the states ran up in the war. Who backed it, and why?
opts: Hamilton, as he wanted strong national power
Henry, as he wanted strong national power
Hamilton, as he wanted the states to keep power
Madison, as he wanted the states to keep power
b.why: Hamilton, as Treasury secretary, wanted the national government to take on the states' war debts, which fitted his support for strong national power. Henry is the tempting wrong choice, but he feared a strong national government, so this plan did not match his views.
b.clue: Which leader ran the nation's money, and what did he want for the national government?

version.title: Leaders of the new nation
card: George Washington
Presided over the Constitutional Convention in 1787 and became the first president in 1789. He usually sided with Hamilton, and set examples for the office, such as serving only two terms.
James Madison

Did much to plan the Constitution, then wrote essays with Hamilton and John Jay urging the states to ratify it. In the 1790s he opposed Hamilton's plans as giving the national government too much power.
Alexander Hamilton
Wanted a strong national government and urged ratification. As Washington's first Treasury secretary, he got it to take on the states' war debts and to set up a national bank.
Patrick Henry
A Virginian who led the fight against ratification in his state in 1788. He feared a strong national government would threaten the liberty of the states and their people.
version.remember: The leaders argued over the national government's power, first over ratifying the Constitution, then over Hamilton's plans.

a.q: In the 1788 debate over ratifying the Constitution, what was Patrick Henry's main objection to it?
opts: He feared it gave the national government too much power
He feared it gave the national government too little power
He thought it gave the state governments too much power
He thought it gave the president too little power to act
a.why: Henry feared that a strong national government would threaten the liberty of the states and their people. The opposite worry, that the national government was too weak, is what led Madison and Hamilton to back the Constitution.
a.clue: Think about what he wanted to protect.

b.q: A student writes that Madison and Hamilton were on opposite sides from the start. Which fact from 1787 and 1788 shows this is wrong?
opts: Both wrote essays that urged ratifying the Constitution
Both feared a strong national government, as Henry did
Both refused to take part in the Constitutional Convention
Both called for keeping the Articles of Confederation
b.why: In 1787 and 1788 Madison and Hamilton were allies who wrote essays urging the states to ratify the Constitution. Their split came later, in the 1790s, over Hamilton's plans as Treasury secretary. It was Henry, not they, who feared a strong national government.
b.clue: Their split came in the 1790s. What were they doing before it?

a.best: He feared it gave the national government too much power

b.best: Both wrote essays that urged ratifying the Constitution
